The Code puts the nurse's first commitment to the client, so it doesn't call for obedience to the provider or loyalty to the employer over the client.

Takeaway: The Code: advocacy, responsibility, accountability, confidentiality.

questions.stem: Halfway through a procedure that she consented to, a client says, “Stop. I've changed my mind.” Which action should the nurse take?
options: Ask her family to persuade her to let the procedure continue
Give her something to help her relax, and then continue
Finish quickly, since she already signed the consent form
Stop, and tell the provider she has withdrawn consent
questions.rationale:
A client can refuse a procedure even after it has begun, without losing her other care. The nurse stops and tells the provider.

A signed form doesn't override a client's withdrawal of consent; continuing could be battery. Asking the family to persuade her, or sedating her to continue, overrides her choice.

Takeaway: Consent can be withdrawn at any time.

questions.stem: At a mass-casualty scene, a triage nurse treats first the clients most likely to survive with quick care, to save the most lives. Which ethical approach should the nurse identify?
options: Utilitarianism
Paternalism
Deontology (duty-based ethics)
Casuistry
questions.rationale:
Utilitarianism judges actions by their consequences: the right act brings the greatest good to the greatest number, as in disaster triage.

Deontology judges by duty and rules, whatever the outcome; casuistry compares similar past cases; and paternalism overrides a person's choice for their supposed good.

Takeaway: The most good for the most people: utilitarianism.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing situations on a unit. Which of them are ethical dilemmas?
options: A nurse is unsure of the right dose of a new medication for a client
Two clients need the last ICU bed, and both have strong claims to it
A nurse disagrees with a coworker about who takes the first lunch break
A competent client refuses a feeding tube; the nurse values his choice and his life
A nurse knows the right action, but the hospital's policy keeps the nurse from taking it
questions.rationale:
An ethical dilemma is a choice between two options that each rest on an ethical principle, with no clearly right answer: autonomy against preserving life, or justice between two clients with strong claims.

Knowing the right action but being blocked from it is moral distress. An unsure dose is a knowledge question, and a lunch schedule isn't an ethical problem.

Takeaway: Dilemma: two right-seeming choices. Moral distress: one right choice, blocked.

questions.stem: When should a nurse ask for an ethics consultation?
options: Whenever a client refuses a treatment the team recommends
When the team and family can't resolve a dilemma about care
Before each end-of-life conversation with a client and family
When a coworker breaks a unit policy, as a first step
questions.rationale:
An ethics committee or consultation helps when the team, client, and family can't resolve a dilemma about care.

A competent client's refusal doesn't need an ethics review, routine end-of-life talks don't either, and a broken policy goes through the chain of command.

Takeaway: Unresolved dilemma: call the ethics committee.

questions.stem: A nurse faces an ethical dilemma about a client's care. Which steps should the nurse take?
options: Identify the values and principles in conflict
Consider the options and their likely outcomes
Act, then evaluate the result
Decide by what the family prefers
Gather the facts of the situation
Follow what most of the staff would do
questions.rationale:
Ethical decision-making is a process: gather the facts, identify the values and principles in conflict, weigh the options and their outcomes, then act and evaluate.

Going by the family's preference or what most staff would do skips the reasoning, and can override the client's rights.

Takeaway: Facts, values, options, act, evaluate.

questions.stem: Two nurses disagree about telling a client bad news. One says, “Honesty is our duty.” The other says, “Holding off will cause the least harm overall.” Which approach should the nurse educator identify in the second nurse's reasoning?
options: Veracity
Deontology (duty-based ethics)
Utilitarianism
Casuistry
questions.rationale:
Weighing which choice causes the least harm overall judges the act by its consequences: utilitarian reasoning.

The first nurse's appeal to duty is deontology. Casuistry compares past cases, and veracity is a principle (truthfulness), not an approach.

Takeaway: Duty: deontology. Consequences: utilitarianism. Past cases: casuistry.

questions.stem: A nurse feels moral distress after a dying client's family insists on aggressive treatment the nurse believes only prolongs suffering. Which actions can help?
options: Talking with a trusted colleague or the nurse manager
Keeping the feelings private, to stay professional
Asking for an ethics consultation
Avoiding clients in similar situations from now on
Using the employee assistance program for support
questions.rationale:
Talking it through, an ethics consultation, and the employee assistance program help a nurse cope with moral distress and can improve the situation.

Bottling it up leads to burnout, and avoiding similar clients doesn't address the distress.

Takeaway: Moral distress: talk, consult, get support.

questions.stem: Which action by a nurse is paternalistic?
options: Offering the client a choice of times for wound care
Asking the client what matters most to her in her care
Explaining the risks of a treatment the client is considering
Holding back a client's diagnosis “for her own good”
questions.rationale:
Paternalism is deciding for someone “for their own good,” like holding back a diagnosis; it overrides the client's autonomy.

Explaining risks, offering choices, and asking what matters to the client all support her autonomy.

Takeaway: “For your own good,” without your say: paternalism.

questions.stem: A nurse thinks, “If I report my near miss, the team will learn and future clients will be safer, even though I'll be embarrassed.” Which ethical approach should the nurse identify in this reasoning?
options: Utilitarianism
Deontology (duty-based ethics)
Casuistry
Paternalism
questions.rationale:
The nurse weighs the outcomes: the most good for the most people (safer future clients) outweighs the nurse's embarrassment, which is utilitarian reasoning.

Deontology would report because it's the nurse's duty, whatever the outcome. Casuistry compares past cases, and paternalism decides for others.

Takeaway: Reasoning by outcomes: utilitarianism.

questions.stem: A nurse is moving to another state. Where should the nurse check what an RN may do there?
options: The ANA's Code of Ethics for Nurses, for the scope
The new state's nurse practice act and board of nursing
The nurse practice act of the state the nurse is leaving
The new employer's job description for RNs
questions.rationale:
Each state's nurse practice act defines nursing and its scope of practice there, and its board of nursing enforces it.

The Code guides ethics, not scope. The old state's act doesn't apply in the new state, and a job description can't go beyond the act.

Takeaway: Scope of practice: the state's nurse practice act.

questions.stem: Which body can discipline a nurse's license?
options: The hospital's human resources office
The Joint Commission
The state board of nursing
The American Nurses Association
questions.rationale:
The state board of nursing, created by the nurse practice act, licenses nurses and can discipline a license to protect the public.

The ANA is a professional association, human resources handles employment, and The Joint Commission accredits organizations; none of them can discipline a license.

Takeaway: Licenses: granted and disciplined by the board of nursing.

questions.stem: A nurse asks whether a hospital's policy can limit what its RNs do more than the state's nurse practice act does. Which response should the nurse manager give?
options: “Yes: a policy can also add tasks the act doesn't allow RNs.”
“No: the federal government, not hospitals, sets the limits on practice.”
“No: policies must match the act exactly, word for word.”
“Yes: a policy can be stricter than the act, but can't widen the scope.”
questions.rationale:
A facility's policy can limit practice further, but it can never widen the scope beyond the state's nurse practice act.

Policies don't have to match the act exactly, and they can't add tasks the act doesn't allow. Nursing practice is regulated by the states.

Takeaway: Policy can narrow the scope, never widen it.

questions.stem: A provider asks a nurse to perform a task the state's nurse practice act doesn't allow RNs to do. Which response should the nurse give?
options: “That's outside the RN scope here. Let's find who can do it.”
“I'll ask another nurse to do it for you instead.”
“I'll do it this once, since you're the one asking.”
“I'll do it if you sign that you take responsibility for it.”
questions.rationale:
The nurse declines, because the task is outside the RN scope under the state's nurse practice act, and helps find someone who's allowed to do it.

A provider's request or signature doesn't change the scope of practice, and handing the task to another nurse doesn't either.

Takeaway: Outside the scope: decline, explain, and help find the right person.

questions.stem: A hospital's electronic records are breached. Which law requires the hospital to tell the affected clients?
options: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)
The Health Information Technology (HITECH) Act
The Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act (EMTALA)
The Uniform Anatomical Gift Act
questions.rationale:
The HITECH Act promoted electronic health records and strengthened HIPAA's rules, including telling clients about breaches.

The ADA protects people with disabilities, EMTALA covers emergency care, and the Uniform Anatomical Gift Act governs organ donation.

Takeaway: HIPAA: privacy. HITECH: electronic records and breach notice.

questions.stem: A client asks what the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (PPACA) does. Which statements should the nurse include?
options: Insurers can't deny coverage for a preexisting condition
It protects the privacy of clients' health records and charts
Young adults can stay on a parent's plan until age 26
It expands access to affordable coverage and preventive care
It makes care free at any hospital in the country
questions.rationale:
The PPACA expanded affordable coverage and preventive care, kept young adults on a parent's plan until 26, and stopped denials for preexisting conditions.

It doesn't make care free at any hospital, and record privacy is HIPAA's job.

Takeaway: PPACA: coverage and access.

questions.stem: A nurse with a hearing impairment asks the employer for an amplified stethoscope. Which law should the nurse manager identify as supporting this request?
options: The Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)
The Americans with Disabilities Act
The nurse practice act
questions.rationale:
The Americans with Disabilities Act protects people with disabilities at work, including reasonable accommodations like an amplified stethoscope.

HIPAA protects health information, the nurse practice act sets the scope of practice, and EMTALA covers emergency care.

Takeaway: Reasonable accommodation, for clients and staff: the ADA.

questions.stem: Off duty, a nurse stops to help at a car crash and starts first aid. Which statement about the nurse's duty is accurate?
options: The nurse may leave once the bleeding slows
The nurse must also ride to the hospital with the injured person
The nurse may leave whenever another bystander arrives
The nurse should stay until someone as qualified or more takes over
questions.rationale:
Under Good Samaritan laws, once a nurse starts helping, the nurse should stay until someone at least as qualified, like EMS, takes over; leaving early could be abandonment.

A bystander without training isn't a safe handoff, and the slowing of the bleeding doesn't end the duty. The nurse doesn't have to ride to the hospital once EMS takes over.

Takeaway: Good Samaritan: help in good faith, within training, and stay until handoff.

questions.stem: During her shift at a clinic, a nurse makes an error and later claims protection under the state's Good Samaritan law. Which statement is accurate?
options: The law doesn't apply, since it covers off-duty emergency help
The law applies if the error was small
The law applies if the clinic is a nonprofit
The law protects her, since she was helping a client
questions.rationale:
Good Samaritan laws limit liability for help given off duty, in an emergency, in good faith. Care given on the job isn't covered.

Helping a client at work, the size of the error, and the clinic's nonprofit status don't bring on-the-job care under the law.

Takeaway: Good Samaritan: off duty, emergency, good faith; not work.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing laws that shape nursing. Which of the following are state laws?
options: EMTALA
The nurse practice act
The Americans with Disabilities Act
Good Samaritan laws
HIPAA
questions.rationale:
The nurse practice act and Good Samaritan laws are passed by each state.

HIPAA, EMTALA, and the ADA are federal laws that apply in every state.

Takeaway: State: nurse practice act, Good Samaritan. Federal: HIPAA, HITECH, EMTALA, ADA, PPACA.

questions.stem: A coworker who forgot her password asks to use a nurse's electronic health record login for a few minutes. Which response should the nurse give?
options: “Sure, just log out when you're done with it.”
“I can't share it; the law protects these records.”
“You can use it if I stay right beside you.”
“Use it, but don't open any of my clients' records.”
questions.rationale:
Each login ties every action in the record to one person. Sharing it breaks the rules for protecting electronic health information (HIPAA, strengthened by HITECH).

Logging out afterward, standing beside her, or limiting which charts she opens doesn't change that her actions would be recorded under the nurse's name.

Takeaway: Never share a login.

questions.stem: A client who has died had registered as an organ donor on his driver's license, but his family objects to donation. Which statement is accurate?
options: The hospital decides, since he can no longer speak for himself
The family's objection overrides his registration as an organ donor
His documented choice stands, under the Uniform Anatomical Gift Act
Donation can go ahead if a court approves it first
questions.rationale:
The Uniform Anatomical Gift Act, the legal base of organ donation, lets a person decide to donate, and that documented decision stands after death.

The family decides only when the person left no decision. A court and the hospital don't decide, since he made his choice.

Takeaway: A documented gift stands; family decides only when there's none.

questions.stem: A client signed the consent for surgery yesterday. This morning he says, “I don't remember agreeing to this. What are they doing to me?” Which action should the nurse take?
options: Explain the surgery to him in detail, then continue the preparations
Ask his family to remind him what he agreed to yesterday
Reassure him that he signed it, and continue the preparations
Hold the preparations, and ask the surgeon to explain it again
questions.rationale:
Consent must be informed. A client who doesn't know what the procedure is hasn't given informed consent, so the nurse holds and asks the surgeon to explain it again.

A signature isn't consent if he doesn't understand. The surgeon, not the nurse, explains the procedure, and the family can't consent for a competent client.

Takeaway: No understanding, no consent: hold and call the provider.

questions.stem: A client wants to name her sister to make health care decisions if she can't. Which document should the nurse tell her about?
options: A durable power of attorney for health care
A do-not-resuscitate order from her provider
A HIPAA release form for her sister
A living will that lists the treatments she wants
questions.rationale:
A durable power of attorney for health care names someone to make decisions if the client can't.

A living will states which treatments she would or wouldn't want, a DNR order is written by the provider, and a HIPAA release lets others receive her information.

Takeaway: Naming a decision-maker: durable power of attorney. Listing wishes: living will.

questions.stem: An unconscious client needs emergency surgery after a crash, and no family can be reached. Which statement is accurate?
options: The surgery waits until a family member signs
The surgery can go ahead under implied consent
The nurse signs the consent form for the client
A court order is needed before any emergency treatment
questions.rationale:
In a true emergency, when the client can't consent and no one can be reached, treatment can go ahead under implied (emergency) consent.

Waiting for family or a court could cost the client's life, and a nurse doesn't sign consent for a client.

Takeaway: Emergency, no one to ask: implied consent.

questions.stem: A client who speaks only Spanish is about to sign a consent form, and her 12-year-old son offers to translate. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Have a bilingual visitor translate
Let the son translate, since the client trusts him
Get a professional medical interpreter
Give her the English form and point to where to sign
questions.rationale:
Informed consent requires that the client understands, so the nurse gets a professional medical interpreter.

A child or a visitor may not translate accurately and can't keep the information private, and a form she can't read isn't informed consent.

Takeaway: Consent in another language: a professional interpreter.

questions.stem: A nurse locks the door of a competent client's room so he can't leave before his tests are done. Which tort should the nurse manager identify?
options: Battery
Invasion of privacy
Assault
False imprisonment
questions.rationale:
False imprisonment is holding a person against their will without legal cause, like locking in a competent client.

Assault is a threat, battery is touching without consent, and invasion of privacy is sharing private information without permission.

Takeaway: Holding a competent person without cause: false imprisonment.

questions.stem: A nurse writes in an email to coworkers that a provider “comes to work drunk,” which isn't true. Which tort should the nurse manager identify?
options: Libel
Assault
Invasion of privacy
Slander
questions.rationale:
Defamation is a false statement that harms someone's reputation. In writing, like an email, it's libel.

Slander is spoken defamation. Assault is a threat, and invasion of privacy is sharing true private information without permission.

Takeaway: Libel: letters (written). Slander: spoken.

questions.stem: A nurse manager is reviewing events on a unit. Which actions could lead to a claim of battery?
options: Keeping a competent client from leaving the unit
Telling a client, “Take this, or I'll hold you down”
Sharing a client's diagnosis with a neighbor
Removing a mole during surgery that the client didn't consent to
Giving an injection the client refused
questions.rationale:
Battery is touching without consent: an injection after a refusal, or a procedure beyond what was consented.

A threat without touch is assault, keeping a client from leaving is false imprisonment, and sharing a diagnosis is invasion of privacy.

Takeaway: Touch without consent: battery. Threat: assault.

questions.stem: Which situation describes malpractice?
options: A visitor's spilled coffee causes a client in the hallway to slip and fall
A nurse gives a drug despite a documented allergy, harming the client
A nurse holds down a client to give a pill he refused
A nurse discusses a client's diagnosis in the elevator
questions.rationale:
Malpractice is negligence by a professional: care below what a reasonably prudent nurse would give, which harms the client, like giving a drug despite a documented allergy.

A visitor's spill is ordinary negligence at most, since a visitor isn't a professional. Holding a client down for a pill he refused is battery, and talking in the elevator is invasion of privacy.

Takeaway: Malpractice: a professional falls below the standard of care, and harm follows.

questions.stem: A nurse gives a client the wrong medication, but it causes no harm. A lawyer says there's no malpractice case. Which element of malpractice is missing?
options: A duty to the client
A breach of the standard of care
Harm to the client
A nursing license
questions.rationale:
Malpractice needs a duty, a breach of the standard of care, harm, and a link between the breach and the harm. Without harm, there's no malpractice claim (though the error still must be reported).

The nurse had a duty to the client, and the wrong medication was a breach. A license isn't one of the elements.

Takeaway: Malpractice: duty, breach, harm, and cause.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the types of torts. Which of the following are quasi-intentional torts?
options: Battery
Invasion of privacy
Negligence
Assault
Defamation
questions.rationale:
Quasi-intentional torts involve no intent to harm, but a voluntary act, often words, that harms: invasion of privacy and defamation.

Battery and assault are intentional torts, and negligence is unintentional.

Takeaway: Intentional: assault, battery, false imprisonment. Quasi-intentional: privacy, defamation. Unintentional: negligence, malpractice.

questions.stem: Two days after surgery, a client refuses to walk, saying it hurts too much. Which action shows beneficence while respecting the client's autonomy?
options: Document the refusal, and skip walking for the rest of the day
Ask the client's family to insist that he get up and walk
Tell the client that walking is required, and help him up right away
Explain why walking helps, treat his pain, and plan the walk with him
questions.rationale:
Beneficence is acting for the client's good: explaining how walking prevents complications and treating the pain first. Planning the walk with him respects his autonomy, since the choice stays his.

Requiring the walk, or having the family insist, overrides his choice. Skipping it without addressing the pain or the reasons gives up on doing good for him.

Takeaway: Do good by informing and removing barriers, not by forcing.

questions.stem: A client says, “I want to complain about how I was treated here.” Which response should the nurse give?
options: “You have the right to make a complaint. I'll help you reach the patient advocate.”
“Let's keep this between us, so it doesn't get anyone in trouble.”
“You'll need to hire a lawyer to raise a concern formally.”
“Raising concerns can affect your care, so it may be better to wait until discharge.”
questions.rationale:
Clients have the right to express complaints and be heard. The nurse supports that right and helps the client reach the patient advocate (or the facility's complaint process).

Suggesting that speaking up could affect care is intimidating and untrue, keeping it quiet blocks the client's right, and a lawyer isn't needed to complain.

Takeaway: Clients may complain and be heard; help them do it.

questions.stem: A nurse is about to witness a client's signature on a surgical consent form. Which findings should the nurse report to the surgeon before the client signs?
options: The client received IV morphine for pain 20 minutes ago
The client's daughter asks to read the form before it's signed
The client asks, “What exactly are they going to remove?”
The client says no one mentioned any other treatment choices
The client is nervous but describes the surgery and its risks
The client is 84 years old and lives alone
questions.rationale:
A client who just had an opioid may not be able to give consent, a client who can't say what the procedure is hasn't been informed, and consent includes the alternatives. The surgeon explains; the nurse holds the signing and tells the surgeon.

Age alone doesn't affect the ability to decide, nervousness is expected in a client who understands the surgery, and a daughter reading the form doesn't change the client's consent.

Takeaway: The nurse witnesses and checks understanding; the provider explains.

questions.stem: A client is admitted to a hospital that takes Medicare. Under the Patient Self-Determination Act, which actions should the nurse take?
options: Record in the chart whether the client has an advance directive
Wait to bring up advance directives until the client is seriously ill
Tell the client an advance directive is needed before admission
Ask the client's family to write an advance directive for the client
Give the client written information about the right to make care decisions
Ask whether the client has an advance directive
questions.rationale:
The Patient Self-Determination Act requires facilities that take Medicare or Medicaid to give written information about clients' rights to make care decisions, refuse treatment, and make an advance directive, to ask whether the client has one, and to record the answer.

An advance directive is voluntary, and care can't depend on having one. Only the client can make it, and asking on admission, while the client can decide, is the point.

Takeaway: PSDA: inform, ask, and record; never require.

questions.stem: A woman in active labor and a man with chest pain arrive at a private hospital's emergency department. Neither has insurance. Under EMTALA, which actions should the nurse expect the hospital to take?
options: Discharge to a free clinic after triage, since neither can pay
Care to stabilize each client's condition before any transfer
A medical screening exam for each client, regardless of ability to pay
Transfer to the public hospital once the lack of insurance is confirmed
A transfer, if needed, only to a hospital that agrees to accept the client
Insurance and payment questions before the screening exam
questions.rationale:
EMTALA requires every emergency department to give anyone who comes in a medical screening exam and stabilizing care, including a woman in labor, whether or not they can pay. A transfer needs a receiving hospital that agrees.

Payment questions can't delay the screening exam, and neither client can be transferred or sent away because they can't pay.

Takeaway: EMTALA: screen, stabilize, then transfer safely, whatever the client can pay.

questions.stem: A nurse educator is reviewing the HITECH Act with new nurses. Which statements should the educator include?
options: “It protects people with disabilities from discrimination.”
“It promoted the use of electronic health records.”
“It requires telling clients when their health information is breached.”
“It requires emergency screening for anyone who comes in.”
“It first gave clients the right to see their own records.”
“It strengthened HIPAA's privacy rules for electronic records.”
questions.rationale:
The HITECH Act came after HIPAA: it promoted electronic health records and strengthened HIPAA's rules for them, including telling clients about breaches.

The right to see one's own records comes from HIPAA, emergency screening from EMTALA, and disability rights from the ADA.

Takeaway: HIPAA = privacy; HITECH = electronic records and breaches.

questions.stem: A nurse is moving from Ohio to New Hampshire. Which should the nurse check in New Hampshire's nurse practice act?
options: The scope of practice for registered nurses in the state
The new hospital's practice of floating nurses between units
The requirements for getting and keeping a license
What can lead to discipline by the board of nursing
The nine provisions of the ANA Code of Ethics
The federal rules for protecting health information
questions.rationale:
Each state's nurse practice act defines nursing and its scope of practice there, sets licensure requirements, and creates the board of nursing, with what can lead to discipline. Its purpose is to protect the public.

The ANA Code of Ethics applies to nurses everywhere and is ethics, not state law. Health information privacy is federal (HIPAA), and floating between units is a hospital policy.

Takeaway: Nurse practice act: the state's scope, licenses, and board.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a malpractice claim filed after a client's fall. Which elements should the nurse identify as needed for the claim to succeed?
options: The injury was caused by the nurse's failure
The client was injured
The nurse meant to cause the client harm
The nurse had a duty to care for the client
The client was unhappy with how the nurse spoke to them
The care fell below what a reasonably prudent nurse would do
questions.rationale:
Malpractice needs all four elements: a duty, a breach of the standard of care (what a reasonably prudent nurse would do), harm, and the breach causing the harm.

Intent to harm belongs to intentional torts like battery, not malpractice, and a client's displeasure isn't harm.

Takeaway: Malpractice: duty, breach, harm, and cause.

questions.stem: A charge nurse is making assignments and deciding which clients get the unit's two bariatric beds. Which actions should the charge nurse take to act on the principle of justice?
options: Assign clients by how much care they need, not by insurance
Tell a client the truth about a delayed test result
Give a client who is in police custody the same care as others
Offer a client a choice of bath time
Give the beds to the clients who need them most
Keep the promise to bring a client's pain medicine in 15 minutes
questions.rationale:
Justice is fairness: care and resources shared by need, and the same care for each client, whatever their insurance or circumstances.

Keeping a promise is fidelity, telling the truth is veracity, and offering a choice is autonomy: all good care, but not justice.

Takeaway: Justice: a fair share, by need.

questions.stem: A nurse is orienting a newly admitted client to the unit. Which rights should the nurse tell the client about?
options: To choose which nurse is assigned to them each shift
To have their health information kept private
To receive any test or treatment they ask for
To refuse a treatment, even one the provider recommends
To know about their condition and their treatments
To voice a concern about their care and have it heard
questions.rationale:
Clients have the right to know their condition and treatments, to make their own decisions, including refusing treatment, to privacy of their information, and to express concerns and be heard.

Clients may choose their doctors, but not a nurse each shift, and the right to decide is the right to accept or refuse, not to receive any treatment they ask for.

Takeaway: Client rights: information, decisions, privacy, respect, and a voice.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to act on provision 3 of the Code of Ethics, advocating for clients. Which actions should the nurse take?
options: Make sure a client's wishes are heard at the care conference
Close the curtain and lower voices when discussing a client's care
Keep quiet about a safety concern to avoid conflict with the team
Give an order the nurse believes is unsafe, since the provider wrote it
Make the decision a client is struggling with, to spare them stress
Report a coworker who seems impaired on duty
questions.rationale:
Provision 3 of the Code: the nurse advocates for and protects the client's rights, health, and safety, like guarding privacy, speaking up about unsafe or impaired practice, and making sure the client's voice is heard.

Deciding for a client takes away their autonomy, and an order the nurse believes is unsafe is questioned, not given. Staying quiet about a safety concern leaves the client unprotected.

Takeaway: Advocacy: protect the client's rights, voice, and safety.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing for a care conference about a client with diabetes who still eats sweets daily. Which statements in the nurse's notes should the nurse identify as facts?
options: “He thinks family meals matter more than his diet plan.”
“He isn't trying to get better.”
“His A1C this morning was 9.6%.”
“He ate two pieces of cake at lunch today.”
“He has missed three of his last four clinic visits.”
“He'd do better if his wife cooked for him.”
questions.rationale:
Facts can be checked and shown true: a lab result, what he ate, and missed visits. Telling them apart from opinions and values is the first step of values clarification.

“Isn't trying” and what would help him are one person's opinions, and what matters more to him is a value. Knowing which is which keeps the nurse's own values from steering his care.

Takeaway: Values clarification: fact, opinion, or value?

questions.stem: A client who was brought to the hospital from the county jail is admitted to a medical unit. The nurse asks how he prefers to be addressed and gives him the same courteous, careful care as every other client. Which provision of the Code of Ethics should the nurse identify?
options: Provision 3: advocating for the client's rights and safety
Provision 1: respect for each person
Provision 6: an ethical work environment
Provision 8: collaborating with other professions and the public
questions.rationale:
Provision 1: the nurse practices with compassion and respect for the inherent dignity and worth of every person, whatever the person's background, circumstances, or condition. Asking how he wants to be addressed and giving him the same care honors that.

Provision 3 isn't the right answer: advocacy protects a client's rights and safety when something threatens them, and nothing here does; the nurse is showing respect. Provision 6 is about the workplace, and provision 8 about working with other professions and the public.

Takeaway: Respect and dignity for every person, whoever they are: provision 1.

questions.stem: A nurse sells vitamin supplements as a side business. A client on the unit asks which supplements might help his recovery. The nurse doesn't offer her products, and suggests he ask his provider. Which provision of the Code of Ethics should the nurse identify?
options: Provision 1: respect for each person
Provision 3: advocating for the client's rights and safety
Provision 7: advancing the profession through research and standards
Provision 2: the client's interests come first
questions.rationale:
Provision 2: the nurse's primary commitment is to the client, so the client's interests come first. When a nurse's own interest, like money from a side business, could pull against the client's, the nurse sets it aside: this is a conflict of interest.

Provision 3 isn't the right answer: it covers protecting a client's rights and safety, as from unsafe or impaired practice, while this is about the nurse keeping her own interests out of the client's care. Provision 1 is respect for each person, and provision 7 is research and standards.

Takeaway: The nurse's own interests never come before the client's: provision 2.

questions.stem: A provider tells a nurse to give a dose the nurse believes is unsafe, saying, “Just give it. It's my responsibility, not yours.” The nurse holds the dose and asks to discuss it, since the nurse answers for every dose the nurse gives. Which provision of the Code of Ethics should the nurse identify?
options: Provision 4: accountability for one's own practice
Provision 2: the client's interests come first
Provision 6: an ethical work environment
Provision 9: the profession's voice for social justice
questions.rationale:
Provision 4: the nurse has authority, accountability, and responsibility for nursing practice. A nurse answers for his or her own judgments and actions, and can't hand that accountability to someone else, even a provider who offers to take it.

Provision 2 isn't the right answer: the client's interests do come first, but what decides this case is that the nurse remains accountable for the dose, whoever ordered it. Provision 6 is the work environment, and provision 9 the profession's voice in policy.

Takeaway: A nurse is accountable for the nurse's own practice and can't pass it to someone else: provision 4.

questions.stem: A staff nurse joins a unit council that reads the latest studies on preventing pressure injuries and turns them into the unit's new practice guidelines. Which provision of the Code of Ethics should the nurse identify?
options: Provision 6: an ethical work environment
Provision 4: accountability for one's own practice
Provision 7: advancing the profession through research and standards
Provision 8: collaborating with other professions and the public
questions.rationale:
Provision 7: nurses advance the profession through research and scholarly inquiry, developing professional standards, and shaping nursing and health policy. Turning new studies into the unit's practice guidelines does exactly that.

Provision 6 isn't the right answer: a council does improve the unit, but provision 6 is about the ethical climate and conditions of work, like safe staffing, while building practice guidelines from research is provision 7. Provision 4 is accountability for one's own practice, and provision 8 is collaborating with other professions and the public.

Takeaway: Research, scholarship, and practice standards: provision 7.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a coalition of physicians, social workers, and city officials that brings free blood pressure screenings to a neighborhood where many residents have untreated hypertension. Which provision of the Code of Ethics should the nurse identify?
options: Provision 8: collaborating with other professions and the public
Provision 1: respect for each person
Provision 6: an ethical work environment
Provision 9: the profession's voice for social justice
questions.rationale:
Provision 8: the nurse collaborates with other health professionals and the public to protect human rights, promote health, and reduce health disparities, like a community coalition bringing screenings to a neighborhood with untreated hypertension.

Provision 9 isn't the right answer: it also concerns social justice, but through the nursing profession's own organizations speaking on policy, while here a nurse works directly with other disciplines and the community. Provision 1 is respect for each person, and provision 6 is the work environment.

Takeaway: Working with other professions and the public to reduce health disparities: provision 8.

questions.stem: Through her state nurses association, a nurse helps prepare testimony for lawmakers that supports a bill expanding health coverage for low-income families. Which provision of the Code of Ethics should the nurse identify?
options: Provision 3: advocating for the client's rights and safety
Provision 6: an ethical work environment
Provision 8: collaborating with other professions and the public
Provision 9: the profession's voice for social justice
questions.rationale:
Provision 9: the profession of nursing, through its professional organizations, speaks for nursing's values and works to bring social justice into nursing and health policy, like a nurses association testifying for wider coverage.

Provision 8 isn't the right answer: it also aims at fairer health, but by collaborating with other professions and the public, while this nurse works through the profession's own association on legislation. Provision 3 is advocacy for one client's rights and safety, and provision 6 is the work environment.

Takeaway: The profession, through its organizations, speaking for social justice in policy: provision 9.

questions.stem: A hospital names a staff nurse the new unit manager, with authority over scheduling, budgets, and hiring. A coworker asks what the new role means for the unit. Which statement by the charge nurse is accurate?
options: “She now holds a formal position, and she'll still need influence to lead us.”
“Her title gives her influence, so staff will follow her plans without persuasion.”
“She's now an informal leader, since her authority comes from her peers.”
“Managing is her job now, so leading the unit falls to the senior staff.”
questions.rationale:
A manager holds an official position in the organization, so management is always formal. Leadership is different: it's the use of interpersonal skills to influence others toward a goal. A new manager has authority, but still has to earn the staff's cooperation by leading.

“Her title gives her influence” isn't the right answer: authority and influence sound alike, but a title gives the right to direct, not the willingness to follow. An informal leader has no official appointment, which isn't the case here. And managing doesn't hand leading to someone else: every nurse, manager or not, is expected to lead.

Takeaway: Management is a formal position; leadership is influence. A good manager needs both.

questions.stem: During a busy night, a staff nurse with no charge role notices a new nurse falling behind, rallies two coworkers to help, and the unit runs smoothly. Coworkers often go to this nurse for advice. Which explanation fits this nurse's role best?
options: A formal leader acting on authority from the unit
A manager carrying out the organizing function for the shift
An informal leader whose influence comes from peers' trust
A charge nurse acting through the chain of command
questions.rationale:
An informal leader isn't appointed to direct others but takes on a leadership role because of who they are: coworkers trust the nurse, ask for advice, and follow when the nurse rallies them.

A manager organizing resources isn't the right answer, even though the nurse did move people to where help was needed. But organizing is a management function, and management is always formal: this nurse holds no official position. A formal leader and a charge nurse both have official authority, which the stem rules out.

Takeaway: No title, but peers follow: that's an informal leader, leading by influence.

questions.stem: A nurse educator teaches a group of new graduate nurses about leadership and management. Which statement by a new graduate indicates an understanding of the teaching?
options: “I'll start building leadership skills once I'm ready for a charge role.”
“I'll lead and manage every shift, starting with my own clients' care.”
“A strong manager becomes a strong leader once the title brings respect.”
“My influence on the team will come mostly from my job title.”
questions.rationale:
All nurses manage and lead in practice: they manage their own clients' care, time, and resources, and they influence coworkers, clients, and families. So every nurse should keep building both skills from the first day.

Waiting for a charge role isn't the right answer, even though leadership sounds like a job title. But leadership doesn't wait for a position. The other two choices tie influence to a title, which mixes up authority (from the position) with influence (from interpersonal skills).

Takeaway: Every nurse leads and manages, starting with their own clients; influence comes from skills, not a title.

questions.stem: A nurse manager and a respected staff nurse both want to shorten call-light response times on their unit. Which action should the nurse manager take, since it needs the manager's formal authority?
options: Share a vision of faster responses with coworkers
Model answering call lights promptly on each shift
Persuade peers to try a no-pass zone for call lights
Change the unit's assignments to add a float aide
questions.rationale:
Changing staff assignments and adding staff means directing others' work and assigning resources, which takes the authority of an official position: that's management.

Sharing a vision isn't the right answer, even though managers do share visions. But a vision, role modeling, and persuasion are tools of leadership, and an informal leader can use all three without any title.

Takeaway: Influence (vision, example, persuasion) is open to any nurse; directing staff and resources takes a manager's formal authority.

questions.stem: A nurse manager is choosing a staff nurse to lead a falls-prevention project, and wants someone coworkers already follow. Which observations should the manager weigh in favor of a staff nurse?
options: Coworkers ask the nurse for advice on difficult cases.
The nurse has more years on the unit than anyone else.
Peers began a bedside safety check after the nurse modeled it.
The nurse explains goals in ways coworkers understand and accept.
The nurse holds the highest certification on the unit.
The nurse follows unit policies closely and rarely needs reminders.
questions.rationale:
Coworkers following a nurse is a sign of influence, the heart of leadership: peers ask the nurse for advice, copy what the nurse models, and accept the goals the nurse explains. An effective leader turns a vision into goals others understand, and acts as a role model.

Following policy closely isn't the right answer: it makes a reliable employee, but complying isn't the same as influencing others. Seniority and certification are worth respecting, but neither one shows that coworkers follow this nurse.

Takeaway: Look for influence (peers seek the nurse out, copy the nurse, accept the nurse's goals), not years, credentials, or compliance.

questions.stem: A nurse manager notices that staff follow a new hourly rounding policy only on the days she's on the unit. Which change in the manager's approach is most likely to make the practice last?
options: Explain why rounding matters and let nurses shape how it's done
Post the policy in the break room and audit rounding each week
Assign one nurse each shift to remind coworkers about rounding
Add rounding to each nurse's annual evaluation so it affects raises
questions.rationale:
Staff comply when the manager is watching because the policy rests on authority alone. Lasting change comes from leadership: a vision staff understand, and a say in how it's carried out, so they own the practice.

Weekly audits aren't the right answer, even though measuring is a real management function (controlling), and it can show the problem. But audits and evaluations tied to raises keep the practice tied to being watched or rewarded, and a reminder nurse just moves the watching to a coworker.

Takeaway: Authority gets compliance while someone's watching; vision and participation get commitment.

questions.stem: A charge nurse lets an experienced, motivated team decide among themselves how to divide the day's work, and checks in only when someone asks. Which leadership style is the charge nurse using?
options: Democratic
Laissez-faire
Bureaucratic
Situational
questions.rationale:
A laissez-faire leader takes a hands-off approach and lets the group decide based on its own expertise. It can work when the group is made up of committed, skilled members, like this team.

Democratic isn't the right answer, even though the team does decide. But a democratic leader stays involved: the leader encourages discussion and coordinates the group's decision. A bureaucratic leader leads by the rules and procedures, and a situational leader adapts the style to each situation.

Takeaway: Hands-off, the group decides alone: laissez-faire. The leader guides a group decision: democratic.

questions.stem: A charge nurse usually asks for the team's input before making decisions. In which situation is the best choice for the charge nurse to make the decisions alone and give direct instructions?
options: Planning the unit's holiday schedule
Choosing a new bedside handoff format
Moving clients during a fire evacuation
Orienting experienced travel nurses to the unit
questions.rationale:
An autocratic leader makes the decisions and directs the activities. It's efficient and focused on the task, which is what an emergency like a fire needs: there's no time for discussion, and everyone must know exactly what to do.

Orienting experienced travel nurses isn't the right answer, even though they're new to the unit. But they're experienced professionals, who do well with explanation and input, not orders. Holiday schedules and a handoff format affect the whole team and aren't urgent, so input builds commitment.

Takeaway: Emergencies and tasks with no time to discuss call for direct, autocratic leadership; otherwise, involve the team.

questions.stem: A nurse manager asks each shift for ideas on reducing falls, leads a discussion of the options, and has the staff choose one together. Which result should the manager plan for?
options: Quick decisions that follow a set protocol
Little need for the manager to coordinate
Close adherence to the existing procedures
More commitment, and a slower decision
questions.rationale:
This is democratic (participative) leadership: the leader encourages discussion and shared decision making, which builds engagement and productivity. Hearing from every shift takes coordination and time, so the decision comes more slowly.

Little need to coordinate isn't the right answer, even though the staff make the choice. But a democratic leader stays involved and coordinates the group; a hands-off leader who doesn't coordinate is laissez-faire. Quick decisions fit an autocratic style, and adherence to procedures a bureaucratic one.

Takeaway: Democratic leadership trades speed for engagement, and needs a leader who coordinates.

questions.stem: Staff on a unit say their manager answers every suggestion with “That's not how the procedure reads,” even when a change would be safe and fit the unit's goals. Which problem is most likely to develop on the unit?
options: Dissatisfaction from the lack of flexibility
Confusion from a lack of clear procedures
Unsafe care from too little supervision of staff
Slow decisions from too many opinions
questions.rationale:
A bureaucratic leader works strictly within the organization's policies and procedures and allows little flexibility, which can leave staff dissatisfied.

Unsafe care from too little supervision isn't the right answer, even though the manager isn't responsive to staff. But this manager supervises closely, by the rules: too little supervision is the risk of a laissez-faire style. Unclear procedures is the opposite of this unit's problem, and slow decisions from many opinions fits a democratic style.

Takeaway: Rules first, little flexibility: bureaucratic leadership, with dissatisfied staff as its risk.

questions.stem: A charge nurse leads two experienced nurses and a new graduate. Midmorning, a client on the unit suddenly deteriorates. Which approach should the charge nurse take with the team today?
options: Let the three nurses organize their own work, as the experienced ones prefer
Direct the team during the emergency, and coach the new graduate closely
Hold a quick team vote before each decision so everyone shares it
Follow the unit's written routine exactly so the new graduate learns it
questions.rationale:
A situational leader adapts the style to the situation and the people: direct leadership while a client is deteriorating, and more guidance for a new graduate than for experienced nurses. Flexibility is the key.

Letting all three organize their own work isn't the right answer: it fits the experienced nurses, but it leaves the new graduate without support and the emergency without direction. A vote is too slow for an emergency, and following the written routine exactly is rigid when the situation has changed.

Takeaway: Match the style to the moment and the person: direct in a crisis, coaching for a novice, hands-off for experts on a routine day.

questions.stem: A charge nurse usually involves the team in decisions. In which situations should the charge nurse give direct instructions instead of asking the team for input?
options: Choosing the theme for the unit's practice council meeting
A smoke alarm sounds and the unit must evacuate
Deciding which shift tries a new break schedule first
Planning next month's staff education topics
A new nurse's client has a falling oxygen saturation
A client on the unit goes into cardiac arrest
questions.rationale:
Direct, autocratic leadership fits emergencies and situations where someone needs clear direction right away: a cardiac arrest, an evacuation, and a new nurse with a client whose oxygen saturation is falling (the novice needs direction, and the client can't wait).

The break schedule isn't the right answer, even though someone has to decide it. But it isn't urgent, and the people affected have useful input, so involving them builds commitment. The council theme and education topics are also good chances for participation.

Takeaway: Urgent and safety-critical, or a novice who needs direction: give direct instructions. Not urgent: involve the team.

questions.stem: A nurse manager's hands-off style worked well with the unit's long-time, skilled staff. After half the staff are replaced by new graduates, missed tasks and near misses increase. Which action should the nurse manager take first?
options: Keep the hands-off style so the new nurses build independence
Ask the staff to vote on how the unit should be led
Give more direction and structure as the new nurses learn
Write a stricter procedure manual and have each nurse sign it
questions.rationale:
A laissez-faire style works only when the group is skilled and committed. The group has changed, and the near misses show it, so the leader adapts (situational leadership): more direction and structure until the new nurses have the skills to work more independently.

A stricter manual isn't the right answer, even though it adds structure. But a rule-based (bureaucratic) fix gives new nurses paperwork, not the direction and coaching they need, and it costs flexibility. Keeping the hands-off style ignores the near misses, and a vote on leadership doesn't help nurses who don't know the work yet.

Takeaway: Hands-off leadership fits experts. When the team changes, the leader's style changes with it.

questions.stem: A nursing student says, “Some people are born leaders, and I'm just not one of them.” Which response by the nurse educator is accurate?
options: “That's often true, since leadership traits are mostly set by adulthood.”
“Leadership comes with a formal title, so you'll learn it once you're promoted.”
“Leaders need a charismatic personality, so focus on your clinical skills.”
“Leadership styles develop through education, training, and experience.”
questions.rationale:
Behavior-based theories hold that leaders develop their style through education, training, and experience, so leadership can be learned.

Leadership traits set by adulthood isn't the right answer: it matches the oldest, trait-based theory (leaders are born with certain traits), which is exactly what the student believes. The class presents behavior-based and later theories, which say leadership is learned. Leadership also doesn't wait for a title, and charisma is one contemporary style, not a requirement.

Takeaway: Trait theory says leaders are born; behavior theory says they're made, through education, training, and experience.

questions.stem: A nurse manager shares a vision of a restraint-free unit, coaches each nurse on alternatives, and asks staff to come up with creative solutions. Staff go well beyond what's required. Which leadership style does the manager's approach fit best?
options: Transformational
Transactional
Charismatic
Laissez-faire
questions.rationale:
A transformational leader motivates the group toward a shared vision, coaches each person (individual consideration), encourages creative problem solving (intellectual stimulation), and often gets performance beyond what's expected.

Charismatic isn't the right answer, even though the manager inspires staff. But a charismatic leader engages the group through personality, while this manager builds the vision, coaches, and asks staff to solve the problem. A transactional leader exchanges rewards for meeting expectations, and a laissez-faire leader steps back.

Takeaway: Vision, coaching, creative problem solving, and results beyond expectations: transformational.

questions.stem: A nurse manager gives staff an extra day off when the unit meets its hand-hygiene audit goal, and corrects nurses when an audit shows a missed step. Which result should the manager expect from this approach?
options: Performance far beyond what's expected
Results that match the expected targets
Little direction, since the manager steps back
Strong loyalty to the manager's personality
questions.rationale:
This is transactional leadership: rewards in exchange for meeting set goals (contingent reward), and correcting errors when monitoring finds them (management by exception). It tends to produce expected outcomes.

Performance far beyond what's expected isn't the right answer, even though rewards motivate. But going beyond expectations is the mark of transformational leadership, which motivates through a shared vision rather than an exchange. Stepping back is laissez-faire, and loyalty to a personality is charismatic.

Takeaway: Transactional leadership gets the expected results; transformational leadership gets more than expected.

questions.stem: A nurse manager's unit has high staff turnover and burnout, and a rising number of medication errors. Based on the leadership research from class, which approach should the nurse manager work to develop?
options: Passive leadership, giving staff more independence
Transactional leadership, linking rewards to the audit results
Transformational leadership, coaching toward a shared goal
Bureaucratic leadership, tightening the unit's procedures
questions.rationale:
Research on nursing leadership links transformational leadership with better staff well-being, higher job satisfaction, less burnout, and a lower intention to leave, and with client outcomes like fewer medication errors and higher satisfaction. That matches all three of this unit's problems.

Transactional leadership isn't the right answer, even though rewards tied to audits can bring error numbers up to target. But it produces expected outcomes, not the retention and well-being this unit needs. Passive (avoidant) leadership is linked to poorer outcomes, and tighter procedures can add to dissatisfaction.

Takeaway: Turnover, burnout, and safety problems point to transformational leadership, the style the research favors.

questions.stem: On a unit's practice council, nurses, a pharmacist, and a physical therapist each lead the agenda items in their own area, and decisions are made together. Which benefit should the unit expect from this structure?
options: Broader decisions that draw on each member's expertise
Faster decisions, since one leader sets the whole direction
Fewer meetings, since members act independently
Clearer authority, through a single chain of command
questions.rationale:
Shared leadership builds on collective action: leadership moves among members, so decisions draw on more people's expertise, a broader decision-making process.

Clearer authority through one chain of command isn't the right answer, even though a council is a formal structure. But shared leadership spreads leadership across members rather than concentrating it. One leader setting the direction is the opposite of shared leadership, and members who act independently aren't sharing decisions.

Takeaway: Shared leadership spreads leading across the team, for broader decisions built on everyone's expertise.

questions.stem: A nurse manager wants to lower turnover and help staff perform beyond expectations. Which actions should the nurse manager take?
options: Meet with each nurse about goals and offer coaching
Rely mainly on bonuses for meeting audit targets
Share a clear picture of what the unit could become
Step back and let staff handle problems on their own
Invite staff to find creative solutions to unit problems
Act with integrity and keep commitments to staff
questions.rationale:
These are the parts of transformational leadership, the style linked to lower turnover and performance beyond expectations: coaching each nurse (individual consideration), an inspiring vision (inspirational motivation), creative problem solving (intellectual stimulation), and integrity that builds trust (idealized influence).

Bonuses for audit targets isn't the right answer, even though rewards do motivate. But rewards in exchange for meeting targets are transactional, and produce expected results, not results beyond them. Stepping back is a passive, laissez-faire approach, linked to poorer outcomes when the team needs leadership.

Takeaway: Vision, coaching, creativity, and integrity are the four parts of transformational leadership.

questions.stem: Staff at a nursing home say the director of nursing is rarely seen on the units and acts only after a problem becomes serious. Staff turnover is high. Which explanation of this leadership is best supported by the research from class?
options: A hands-off style that works because the staff are experienced
A passive, avoidant style linked to poorer outcomes for staff
A transactional style that corrects errors after they happen
A bureaucratic style focused mainly on the facility's rules
questions.rationale:
Acting only once problems become serious, and being largely absent, is passive-avoidant leadership: passive management by exception and laissez-faire, an absence of leadership. Research found this style far too common in nursing homes, and linked it to poorer leadership outcomes, while transformational leadership is linked to staying on the job.

Transactional correction of errors isn't the right answer, even though the director does react to problems. But a transactional leader monitors actively and corrects errors as they're found; this director waits until problems are serious. A hands-off style that works needs a committed, stable team, and the high turnover says this one isn't working.

Takeaway: Active monitoring and correction is transactional; waiting until problems are serious is passive-avoidant, the style linked to the worst outcomes.

questions.stem: A nurse manager compares the unit's monthly fall rate with the target set in January, and gives staff feedback on the results. Which management function is the manager carrying out?
options: Planning
Organizing
Controlling
Coordinating
questions.rationale:
Controlling uses measures to monitor and evaluate progress toward goals: setting a performance standard, comparing actual results with it, and giving feedback.

Planning isn't the right answer, even though a target was involved. But setting the target in January was planning; comparing this month's results with it is controlling. Organizing assigns staff, equipment, and supplies, and coordinating (directing) motivates people and delegates work.

Takeaway: Set the goal: planning. Measure results against it and give feedback: controlling.

questions.stem: Before flu season, a nurse manager writes a staffing plan to put in place if more than a fifth of the staff call out sick at once. Which kind of plan has the manager written?
options: A strategic plan
An operational plan
A budget plan
A contingency plan
questions.rationale:
A contingency plan prepares for something that may happen, based on how likely it is, like a wave of staff illness during flu season.

A strategic plan isn't the right answer, even though it's also prepared in advance. But a strategic plan sets the organization's long-term outcomes, usually through a committee that gathers data from stakeholders over months. An operational plan carries out day-to-day work, and a budget plans spending.

Takeaway: “If this happens, we'll do that” is a contingency plan; long-term organizational goals are a strategic plan.

questions.stem: The hospital has approved four new beds on a unit. The nurse manager works out which staff, equipment, and supplies will go to the new beds, and who will report to whom. Which management function is the manager carrying out?
options: Organizing
Controlling
Coordinating
Planning
questions.rationale:
Organizing is identifying and assigning resources, from staff to equipment and supplies, and setting out who reports to whom in the structure.

Planning isn't the right answer, even though it all happens before the beds open. But the decision to add the beds was the plan; arranging the people and things to carry it out is organizing. Controlling measures results against standards, and coordinating motivates people and delegates work as it's done.

Takeaway: Deciding the goal and the course of action is planning; lining up the staff, equipment, and structure to do it is organizing.

questions.stem: At the start of a shift, the charge nurse explains the day's goals to the team, delegates tasks to the assistive personnel, and encourages everyone to keep each other updated. Which management function is the charge nurse carrying out?
options: Organizing
Coordinating
Controlling
Planning
questions.rationale:
Coordinating (directing) uses communication to motivate the group and move the work forward, and delegation is part of it.

Organizing isn't the right answer, even though assignments are involved. But organizing identifies and assigns resources; here the charge nurse is communicating, motivating, and handing off tasks as the work begins, which is directing. Controlling measures results, and planning sets the goals.

Takeaway: Communicating, motivating, and delegating while the work goes on is coordinating (directing).

questions.stem: A hospital's leaders want to improve the hospital's nursing outcomes over the next five years. Which step should the leaders take first?
options: Have the chief nursing officer write the plan and announce it
Have each unit manager set its own goals for the year
Form a committee that gathers data from stakeholders
Have the staff vote on the goal at a staff meeting
questions.rationale:
This is a strategic plan: it focuses on the organization's outcomes. Planning starts from assessment data, and a strategic plan usually involves a committee working over several months to gather and analyze data from stakeholders.

Having the chief nursing officer write the plan isn't the right answer, even though leaders are responsible for the strategy. But writing it before gathering data skips the assessment that planning is built on, and leaves out the stakeholders. Unit goals are short-term and fragmented, and a vote chooses a goal without the data to support it.

Takeaway: Planning starts with assessment data; a strategic plan comes from a committee gathering data from stakeholders.

questions.stem: A nurse manager's unit has a goal of cutting central line infections in half this year. Which actions should the nurse manager take to find out whether the unit is meeting the goal?
options: Order more central line dressing kits
Set a monthly infection rate as the standard
Assign a nurse to each line-care task
Compare each month's rate with the standard
Give staff feedback on the results
Draft next year's budget for supplies
questions.rationale:
Finding out whether a goal is being met is controlling: set a performance standard, compare actual results with it, and give feedback.

Ordering more dressing kits isn't the right answer, even though supplies help prevent infections. But that's organizing resources; it doesn't tell the manager whether the goal is being met. Assigning tasks is directing, and next year's budget is planning.

Takeaway: Controlling is a loop: a standard, a comparison with real results, and feedback.

questions.stem: A new nurse asks the preceptor how being accountable differs from being responsible. Which statement by the preceptor matches the definitions from class?
options: “You're responsible to your scope of practice, and accountable for your duties.”
“They mean the same thing in nursing, though managers use them differently.”
“Managers are accountable for outcomes, while staff nurses are responsible for tasks.”
“You're accountable to your scope of practice, and responsible for your duties.”
questions.rationale:
In the class's definitions, a nurse is accountable to something, like the scope of practice, and responsible for carrying out their professional roles and duties.

The first choice isn't the right answer: it uses the same two pieces with the words swapped. Accountable to the standard, responsible for the work. The two terms aren't the same, and both apply to every nurse, not just to managers or just to staff.

Takeaway: Accountable to (the scope of practice); responsible for (your duties).

questions.stem: A charge nurse asks a staff nurse to take the next admission. The staff nurse says, “You're a nurse just like me. You can't tell me what to do.” Which statement about the charge nurse's authority is accurate?
options: The facility gives the charge role the right to direct others' work
Authority comes from seniority, so it depends on years of service
The charge nurse can direct the assistive personnel, but not nurses
Assigning admissions belongs to the nurse manager, not the charge nurse
questions.rationale:
Authority is the right to direct others and their activities to reach outcomes. It comes from the organization: the facility gives the charge role that right, in line with its chain of command.

Authority from seniority isn't the right answer, even though experienced nurses often have influence. But influence and authority are different: authority comes with the position, not the years. A charge nurse directs nurses as well as assistive personnel, and making assignments during the shift is part of the role.

Takeaway: Authority comes from the position the organization gives; influence comes from the person.

questions.stem: Two nurses on a unit have argued about lunch breaks for weeks, and coworkers have started taking sides. Which action should the nurse manager take first?
options: Schedule the two nurses on different shifts for the next month
Meet with both nurses to hear each side and agree on a plan
Write a break policy and post it for the whole unit
Refer both nurses to the employee assistance program
questions.rationale:
Managing conflict is one of a manager's principles, and conflict on a team affects everyone. The first step is to bring the two nurses together, hear each side, and reach an agreement on next steps, which keeps the conflict healthy and resolves it at its source.

Writing a break policy isn't the right answer, even though it addresses the topic. But a policy imposed without talking to the people in conflict leaves the conflict itself unresolved. Separating the nurses avoids it, and the employee assistance program may help later, but it hands off a work problem the manager should address first.

Takeaway: Address conflict directly with the people involved, before rules, reassignments, or referrals.

questions.stem: Halfway through the year, a nurse manager sees that the unit's supply spending is well above the projected budget. Which action should the nurse manager take?
options: Reduce the float staff hours to balance the budget
Ask staff to borrow supplies from other units
Review where costs differ from the projection and adjust
Request a larger budget for next year and keep spending as is
questions.rationale:
Managing resources means knowing how the budget affects care, and adapting when actual expenses differ from the projected ones. So the manager finds out where and why costs differ, and changes practices to match best practice.

Cutting float staff hours isn't the right answer, even though it balances the numbers quickly. But it takes from staffing, which affects safe care, to fix a supply problem it doesn't explain. Borrowing supplies moves the cost elsewhere, and asking for more next year doesn't manage this year's spending.

Takeaway: When actual costs differ from the budget, find the cause and adjust; don't fix one resource by cutting another.

questions.stem: A nurse manager wants to improve staff engagement and the unit's outcome measures. Which actions should the nurse manager take?
options: Involve staff in choosing how to improve a quality measure
Make unit decisions alone so staff can focus on care
Help each team member understand the group's purpose
Address conflicts between staff members early
Wait for staff to ask for help before stepping in
Plan the workday so time goes to the top priorities
questions.rationale:
The principles of management include enhancing performance through staff engagement and participation, building teams whose members understand the group's purpose, managing conflict, and managing time.

Making decisions herself so staff can focus on care isn't the right answer, even though it sounds considerate. But it takes away the participation that builds engagement and improves outcome measures. Waiting for staff to ask for help is passive: problems grow before the manager acts.

Takeaway: Engage staff, build the team around a shared purpose, address conflict early, and manage time.

questions.stem: A hospitalist asks a cardiologist to see a client and advise on managing the client's new atrial fibrillation. The hospitalist stays in charge of the client's care. Which kind of request has the hospitalist made?
options: A transfer of care
A referral
A handoff
A consultation
questions.rationale:
In a consultation, one provider formally asks another for input or advice on how to approach or treat a condition, and keeps managing the client.

A referral isn't the right answer, even though the terms are often used interchangeably. But in a referral, the provider hands responsibility for managing the condition to the other provider. A transfer of care turns all of the client's care over to another provider, and a handoff passes information and responsibility at a shift change or transition.

Takeaway: Consult: advice, and the first provider stays in charge. Referral: the condition's management moves. Transfer: all care moves.

questions.stem: A client's primary care provider sends the client to a wound specialist, who will now manage the client's foot ulcer, while the primary care provider keeps managing the client's other conditions. The client's daughter asks the nurse what happened. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Your mother has been referred to the specialist for her ulcer.”
“The specialist is consulting, so your mother's provider decides.”
“Your mother's care has been transferred to the specialist.”
“The specialist will advise, and her provider will treat the ulcer.”
questions.rationale:
In a referral, one provider gives another the responsibility for managing a specific condition: the specialist now manages the ulcer, and the primary care provider keeps the rest.

“Transferred” isn't the right answer, even though the ulcer's care moved. But a transfer of care turns over all of the client's care, and here the primary care provider still manages the other conditions. A consultation (the second and fourth choices) means the specialist only advises, while the first provider keeps managing the condition.

Takeaway: One condition's management moves to another provider: referral. Everything moves: transfer. Advice only: consultation.

questions.stem: A hospital's error reviews keep finding that nurses, pharmacists, and therapists each knew part of a problem, but no one put the pieces together. Which change should the hospital's education council make?
options: Train each discipline separately on its own procedures
Train the disciplines in shared classes and drills
Write more detailed safety policies for each department
Make the provider the single decision maker for care
questions.rationale:
Health professionals educated in silos, only within their own discipline, is one of the things that keeps medical errors going. Training the disciplines together builds the shared understanding and communication that interprofessional teams need.

More detailed department policies isn't the right answer, even though policies feel like a safety fix. But they strengthen the silos instead of connecting them. Separate training is the silo itself, and a single decision maker loses what each discipline brings.

Takeaway: Errors that fall between disciplines call for interprofessional education and teamwork, not more silos.

questions.stem: A hospital is building an interprofessional education program on the Interprofessional Education Collaborative (IPEC) core competency areas. Which areas should the program cover?
options: Teams and teamwork
Values and ethics for interprofessional practice
Discipline-specific skills checkoffs
Billing for each discipline's services
Roles and responsibilities
Interprofessional communication
questions.rationale:
IPEC's core competency has four areas: values and ethics for interprofessional practice, roles and responsibilities, interprofessional communication, and teams and teamwork.

Discipline-specific skills checkoffs isn't the right answer, even though every team member needs skills. But checkoffs within one discipline are silo training, not interprofessional competency. Billing isn't part of the competency.

Takeaway: IPEC's four areas: values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teamwork.

questions.stem: A client recovering from a stroke wants to go home and walk to the mailbox. The nurse, physical therapist, occupational therapist, and dietitian each have their own plan, and the plans don't line up. Which action by the nurse best supports collaborative care?
options: Follow the nursing plan and let each discipline follow its own
Ask the provider to decide which discipline's plan comes first
Suggest a team meeting, with the client, to set shared goals
Email the nursing plan to the other disciplines to review
questions.rationale:
Collaborative care is client-centered: the disciplines come together, bring their knowledge and skills, and work toward a common goal with the client, who is always part of the team.

Emailing the nursing plan isn't the right answer, even though it shares information. But it's one-way, and it doesn't make the goals shared. Following separate plans is working in silos, and asking the provider to pick one plan loses the other disciplines' expertise and the client's voice.

Takeaway: Collaboration means one set of goals, built together, with the client at the table.

questions.stem: A provider calls a nurse with a telephone prescription for a new medication for a client. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Repeat it aloud to the provider, then write it in the record later
Ask the provider to text the prescription to the unit's phone
Write it down, and confirm it with the provider at morning rounds
Write it down, read it back as written, and get the provider's OK
questions.rationale:
For a telephone prescription, the nurse records it, reads it back exactly as written to the prescriber, and gets the prescriber's verification (receive, record, read back).

Repeating it aloud isn't the right answer, even though it sounds like a read-back. But the class's rule is to read back what you wrote, not repeat what you heard, since the error can happen in the writing. Confirming at rounds leaves an unverified prescription in the meantime, and a text is not how prescriptions are received.

Takeaway: Record, read back from what you wrote, verify: don't just repeat it.

questions.stem: A nurse calls a provider about a client who had a hip replacement this morning, using SBAR. Which statement should the nurse make for the Assessment part of the call?
